prize_parts.citation: For a visionary Romanian prose oeuvre that builds whole inner cosmologies from memory, the body and dream, with its origin in poetry.

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: Mircea Cărtărescu alone. The wording of the citation has changed. In round 1 I wrote 'with roots in poetry'. After the exchange I would anchor the citation on the prose, with poetry named as the origin of the project and not as a separately assessed pillar. Carlberg argued for this, and Mattson's point that the poetry-as-base claim is a hypothesis supports it. Our evidence on the poetry is thinner than on the novels. The literary case still rests on the common criteria and not on the opening convergence. The voice is distinctive. Public knowledge of the Orbitor sequence (published in English as Blinding) and Solenoid suggests long architectural structures, recurring image systems, and memory, the body and dream treated as a metaphysical subject. Solenoid is widely regarded as a late culmination, so I see no problem of premature judgment. A single-name citation is clean and does not depend on national symbolism, on one title or on a period label. I hold this as a literary argument that has to survive the strongest alternatives. It is not a settled outcome.
statement.case_against: The reservation that weighs most for me remains durability. Palm's test is whether the long novels develop their image systems or only recirculate them. I cannot settle it from reputation and translation. If a reader of the Romanian originals or of Romanian-language criticism showed that the later volumes mainly extend the earlier patterns, my confidence in sustained quality across the whole body of work would fall. I also judge the density, rhythm and musicality of the Romanian prose only indirectly. The poetry and early work are thinly covered in translation, so the claim of one coherent oeuvre across genres is partly inferred. Finally, Sward's point stands that a committee valuing the reinvention of a language or genre over the expansion of a visionary mode could weigh Adonis or Tawada differently. I take that as a legitimate difference in how the criteria are weighted and not as a refutation.

responses.point: Palm asks whether the late novels deepen their image systems or only recirculate them. She sees a visible arc from the poetry through the Blinding sequence to Solenoid, and applies the same rigor-versus-repetition test to Cărtărescu and to Can Xue.
responses.response: I accept the test and the symmetry. The arc she describes is the best argument for sustained quality, but from public knowledge it remains an impression and not something I have checked in the texts. I would not use it to wave away the repetition worry. It is also why I do not rank Can Xue below him on the grounds of sameness alone. Her consistent method may be deepening, and partial translation prevents me from seeing it. I therefore keep Can Xue as a serious alternative. I still prefer Cărtărescu because the evidence of development within one project is firmer for him, not because the question has been closed.

responses.point: Carlberg proposes anchoring the citation on the novels, with poetry as the origin of the vision and not an independently assessed pillar, because translation coverage of the poetry is thin.
responses.response: I adopt this. It is the main change in my file. The chair's summary asked round 2 to settle one wording basis, and prose-first is the more defensible one. It names what we can honestly weigh and still acknowledges the poetic origin without resting a lifetime citation on it. I would add that the wording should avoid implying a verified unity across genres. 'Origin in poetry' says less than 'prose and poetry jointly', and that restraint suits the evidence.

responses.point: Sward notes that if the committee valued formal reinvention of a language or genre over expansion of an established visionary mode, Tawada or Adonis would have a stronger claim. She endorses separating Adonis's poems from his public positions.
responses.response: I take the framing seriously, and it is the sharpest challenge to my preference. Adonis's case, the remaking of Arabic poetic language through myth and fragmentation over some seven decades, is the strongest on reinvention. That is why he is one of my alternatives. I am not persuaded that Cărtărescu's work is only expansion of a mode. The scale and patterning of the books seem to me to be a formal achievement of their own. But I cannot demonstrate that from Arabic or Romanian, and I accept that a reasonable reader could weigh the criteria the other way. Whatever the weighting, the Adonis citation would have to rest on the poems and poetics and not on his public commentary.

responses.point: Sem-Sandberg ranks Can Xue eighth because decades of unchanged method raise a question about development. He cannot separate Adonis's historical influence from the quality of the poems themselves.
responses.response: On Can Xue I still read the consistency as distinctiveness, but I concede that the burden of showing variation in consciousness and social space across her work has not been met on our evidence. That is an evidentiary gap and not a verdict. On Adonis your distinction between influence and the poems is the right discipline. Influence is documented, but a citation has to rest on the texts. If members with real access to the Arabic cannot speak to their formal quality, I would not push him past my alternatives either. The disagreement between us is smaller than the ranking gap suggests, since neither of us can settle it from translation.

responses.point: Mattson calls the claim that poetry is the base of the prose project a hypothesis and not an established fact. She also asks that Cărtărescu's standing rest on the prose and not on a role as a representative of Romanian or European letters.
responses.response: I agree on both. This is why the revised citation names the prose as the achievement and treats poetry as origin only. I also agree about representation: the citation should say nothing about a nation or a region. The chair's summary asked whether any member would prefer no award (P000). I would not. The limits of secondhand judgment apply to every candidate on the list, and they do not single out Cărtărescu. If the committee felt those limits were disqualifying, that would argue for deferring to readers of the original language and not for withholding the prize.

uncertainties: How much of the density, musicality and rhythm of Cărtărescu's Romanian prose survives translation, and whether the longest novels deepen their image systems or recirculate them.
Translation coverage of his poetry, essays and early work, which makes a claim of one coherent oeuvre across genres partly inferred and is the reason the citation is now prose-first.
Whether Can Xue's consistent method over a very large, only partly translated output reflects rigor or repetition.
For Adonis, how far the formal achievement in Arabic prosody can be judged through translation, and how to keep his public positions out of the literary case.
How to define a Carson citation around original poetry and essays, apart from scholarship, translation and book-design, and whether many short works carry enough cumulative weight.

Whether the reinvention of a language or genre should weigh more than large-scale visionary construction under the common criteria. This depends on how members weight the criteria and is not resolved here.
I have not read the corpus for this exercise or independently verified any bibliography. I rely on general public knowledge of the named works and on colleagues' stated views.
statement.conflict_note: No connection to any shortlisted writer is documented in my supplied profile. My scholarly and poetic interests (modern poetry, the fragment, exile literature, Celan) are context and not evidence of preference. I am the chair, I support B026 and I wrote the round-1 chair summary, which reports only positions explicit in the six round-1 files. Carlberg's committee voting status is undocumented and her simulated vote is a modeling assumption. These points are disclosed and not adjudicated.
